The Command Module was the only piece of Apollo that came home — everything else was spent and thrown away along the route. That made it the part that could not fail on reentry, and reentry from the Moon was the hardest version of the problem: the capsule met the atmosphere at nearly eleven kilometres a second, half again as fast as anything returning from Earth orbit, wrapped in a fireball hot enough to boil steel. Its answer was an ablative heat shield engineered to char and peel away in a controlled way, carrying the heat off with it. Block II was the version that flew crews — the ground-up redesign forced by the Apollo 1 fire — and it brought every astronaut who set out for the Moon back alive.

The lunar-capable Command and Service Module that carried Apollo astronauts to lunar orbit between 1968 and 1972. Fifteen crewed flights in total: Apollo 7–17 (eleven Moon-targeted missions), three Skylab crew rotations (1973–1974), and the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz Test Project — including Apollo 13’s improvised lifeboat configuration.
First crewed Apollo flight — Earth-orbit CSM shakedown
First humans to leave low Earth orbit + orbit the Moon
First humans on another celestial body
First crewed LM flight — Earth-orbit LM separation + rendezvous tests
Full lunar-landing dress rehearsal — LM descended to ~14.4 km altitude
Second crewed Moon landing — pinpoint touchdown 163 m from Surveyor 3
The mission that turned a near-disaster into NASA's most celebrated rescue
Third lunar landing — Apollo 13's lost target reached; Shepard's golf shots
First J-mission — extended stay, first Lunar Roving Vehicle, "Genesis Rock"
Last crewed mission to the Moon (and the only Apollo with a trained geologist)
First Moon landing in the lunar highlands — Descartes; John Young's "lunar Grand Prix"
First crewed Skylab visit — repaired the damaged workshop and saved the programme
Second Skylab crew — 59 days, deployed twin-pole solar shield to replace parasol
Longest Skylab stay — 84 days, observed Comet Kohoutek, disputed "Skylab strike" rest day
First international human spaceflight cooperation; first US-USSR rendezvous + docking
Lifted Apollo 7, Skylab crews, and ASTP
NASA pad at Cape Canaveral (1961-68) — first Saturn I; Apollo 1 fire site 1967-01-27; Apollo 7 first crewed launch 1968-10-11
Launched Apollo 8, 9 and 11–17 (Apollo 9 in Earth orbit; Apollo 10 flew from 39B); today flies Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, and Crew Dragon
First crewed lunar lander; Eagle, Antares, Falcon...
Apollo 10 + Skylab + 53 Shuttle flights; now NASA's SLS / Artemis pad
First Soyuz generation; Komarov's fatal flight
Original Apollo CSM design — never flew crewed; killed Apollo 1 crew on the pad 1967-01-27. Redesign produced the Block II flown 1968-1975
Two-person crew; rendezvous and EVA practice
OV-101 — prototype Shuttle. Renamed from Constitution after Star Trek fan campaign. Flew 1977 atmospheric tests; never reached orbit
OV-102 — the first Shuttle orbiter to fly to space (STS-1, 1981-04-12); lost on re-entry STS-107 2003-02-01

The first humans on the Moon. Watched live by ~600 million people — roughly one in six people on Earth at the time. The laser retroreflector placed by Armstrong and Aldrin still receives pulses today, measuring the Earth-Moon distance to millimetre precision. Footprints in the airless regolith will survive unchanged for a million years.

The precision landing — Conrad touched down within ~163 m of the uncrewed Surveyor 3 probe (1967). They retrieved pieces of it for return to Earth, showing spacecraft survive years on the Moon undamaged by radiation or micrometeorites. A proof-of-concept for future rendezvous missions.

Alan Shepard, the first American in space (1961), became the only person to play golf on the Moon. He smuggled a club head and two balls aboard. He claimed one 'went miles and miles' — LRO images suggest about 37 m (40 yards). Still: the furthest sporting achievement in history.

First mission with the Lunar Roving Vehicle — drove 27.9 km. Scott left a small aluminium figurine, 'Fallen Astronaut', and a plaque listing all astronauts and cosmonauts who died in the space race. It is the only artwork on the Moon, left without public announcement at the time.

The only mission to land in the lunar highlands. Charles Duke left a photo of his family sealed in a bag on the lunar surface. On the back he wrote: 'This is the family of Astronaut Duke from Planet Earth. Landed on the Moon, April 1972.' It will outlast civilisation.

The last time humans visited the Moon. Gene Cernan was the last person to walk on its surface. Before climbing the ladder, he said: 'We leave as we came, and God willing, we shall return.' Harrison Schmitt, the only trained geologist on the Moon, collected samples that reshaped our understanding of lunar geology.
